title: India Just Quarantined a Suspected Ebola Patient in Bengaluru. The US and Canada Have Banned Travellers From Three African Countries. Here Is What Every NRI Needs to Know.
excerpt: The WHO has declared a global health emergency. India has launched airport screening. If you have family travelling between India and East Africa, the rules changed overnight.
body:
The World Health Organization declared the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on May 17. As of May 26, more than 900 suspected cases and over 220 deaths have been reported across the DRC, Uganda, and South Sudan. The strain is Bundibugyo — rare, with no approved vaccine and no proven treatment. It is the third-largest Ebola outbreak on record, and it is accelerating.

For the Indian diaspora, this stopped being a distant African crisis last week.

## India's First Suspected Case

A woman travelling from Uganda was quarantined in Bengaluru after presenting symptoms consistent with Ebola. She had arrived via Ahmedabad, and Indian health authorities isolated her within hours. Test results were pending at the time of the quarantine. Health Minister J.P. Nadda confirmed that India has activated screening and surveillance at all international airports and border entry points, and issued advisories on quarantine protocols.

The Ministry of Health has urged all Indian citizens to avoid non-essential travel to the DRC, Uganda, and South Sudan. This is not a suggestion buried in a government circular. It is an active advisory that affects travel insurance, employer policies, and visa conditions for anyone in the diaspora with business or family ties to East Africa.

## The Global Travel Lockdown Is Real

The United States imposed its first-ever Ebola-related travel ban on May 18. Non-citizens who have visited the DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan within the past 21 days are barred from entering the country. On May 23, the ban was extended to include green card holders. Canada followed with a 90-day block on residents from all three countries, effective May 30. Canadian citizens returning from those nations must quarantine for 21 days.

Singapore, Thailand, Jordan, Bahrain, Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, Mexico, and the Cayman Islands have all imposed their own restrictions — ranging from mandatory health screenings to outright entry bans. The list is growing daily.

The Trump administration has taken the extraordinary step of announcing that Americans exposed to Ebola in Africa will be sent to Kenya for quarantine and treatment, not brought home. This marks a sharp departure from previous outbreak protocols and has drawn criticism from infectious disease specialists who call the plan "reckless" and "possibly unlawful."

## Why This Strain Is Different

The Bundibugyo strain that is driving this outbreak is not the Zaire strain that killed 11,000 people in West Africa between 2014 and 2016. Its fatality rate is lower — roughly 30 to 40 per cent compared to Zaire's 50 to 90 per cent — but it comes with a dangerous trade-off. Lower fatality means more survivors who remain mobile and potentially infectious. The virus spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids, and in eastern Congo, where hospitals have been attacked and isolation tents burned by communities reclaiming bodies, containment has been nearly impossible.

There is no vaccine for this strain. The existing Ebola vaccines — rVSV-ZEBOV and Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo — were developed for the Zaire strain and have not been tested against Bundibugyo. Diagnostic capacity is limited. The WHO is scaling up laboratory networks in the DRC, but the infrastructure gap remains enormous.

## What NRIs Should Do Right Now

**If you have travel plans to East Africa**, cancel or postpone them. India's advisory covers the DRC, Uganda, and South Sudan, but the outbreak zone is fluid. Rwanda and Kenya, which border the affected countries, have imposed their own measures but remain accessible transit hubs. Any travel through these corridors now carries screening, quarantine, and potential denial-of-entry risks.

**If you have family in India who recently returned from Africa**, ensure they are aware of the 21-day monitoring window. Ebola's incubation period is 2 to 21 days. Symptoms include sudden fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat, followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, and in some cases, internal and external bleeding.

**If you are an NRI in the US or Canada**, be aware that your immigration status may affect your re-entry if you travel to the affected countries. Green card holders are now included in the US ban. Canadian permanent residents face the 90-day block.

**If you work in healthcare, humanitarian aid, or international logistics**, your employer's travel insurance and evacuation policies may have changed. The US decision to divert Ebola patients to Kenya rather than repatriate them has implications for any American working in the region.

## The Funding Crisis Behind the Crisis

This outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of the worst global health funding environment since 2009. The WHO is seeking one billion dollars for its 2026 health emergency appeal. The United States, historically the largest single donor to global health emergencies, has dramatically reduced its funding commitments. The result is a response apparatus that was already stretched thin before the first Ebola case was confirmed.

For the Indian diaspora — which sends more remittances to Africa than any other Asian community, which staffs hospitals and clinics across East Africa, which runs businesses from Kampala to Kinshasa — this is not an abstract policy failure. It is a direct threat to the networks that connect India to the continent.

The 21-day incubation window is ticking. The airport screening is active. The travel bans are expanding. The time to act is before the next flight, not after.
